passage:
Class 3B observation note, written by Darshan, class teacher.
Chaitanya stood beside my desk at every break this week, asking, "Sir, you're not angry with me, na?" Four or five times a day. Some colleagues call it a bid for attention. I don't think so; he looks tense until I answer.
What I did: I told him warmly each time that I'm not angry. Then I gave him a small job: taking the attendance register to the office alone and coming back to tell me. On Monday he ran both ways. By Friday he walked, and stopped to chat with Irfan on the stairs.
Next step: one break a day at the swings, with me waving from the window.

qa.q: What job did the teacher give Chaitanya?
qa.a: Taking the attendance register to the office alone and coming back to tell him.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's question "you're not angry with me, na?" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He seems anxious and needs to be sure his teacher is still on his side; he looks tense until he gets an answer.

qa.q: What choice did Darshan make instead of treating it as a bid for attention, and why did it work?
qa.a: He answered warmly each time and added a small solo job, so Chaitanya felt safe and slowly grew braver.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the trip to the office by Friday?
qa.a: It likely feels less scary and more his own, since he walks calmly and stops to chat with Irfan.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy who shadows him and needs repeated reassurance, and responds with steady warmth and small steps toward independence.

passage: 14 March. Asif followed me round the school library again today like a small shadow, holding a book he wasn't reading. "Arnab sir, are you staying here the whole period?" Three times he asked. The PT teacher laughed and said the boy just wants attention. Maybe. But his shoulders dropped each time I said yes. So I said yes, kindly, every time. Then I asked him to shelve the red-spine books in the far corner and come show me when he'd done five. He looked back twice, but he did it. Tomorrow, ten books. Small steps. Note to self: ask his mother how mornings go at home.

qa.q: Which books did Arnab ask Asif to shelve?
qa.a: The red-spine books in the far corner.

qa.q: How can you tell that Asif was anxious rather than just seeking attention?
qa.a: He kept asking if Arnab would stay, and his shoulders dropped with relief each time he heard yes.

qa.q: What small independence step did Arnab choose, and why does it suit Asif?
qa.a: He asked Asif to shelve five books in the far corner and come back, a short, safe distance that can grow to ten tomorrow.

qa.q: How does the PT teacher see Asif differently from Arnab?
qa.a: The PT teacher sees a boy wanting attention, while Arnab notices the relief in Asif's shoulders and answers with warmth.

grounding: A teacher's diary shows a boy who shadows him and needs reassurance, met with steady warmth and a small step toward independence.

passage: Every morning at the village school near Sehore, Jaya waited at Anjali-teacher's elbow instead of joining the line. She followed Anjali to the staff room, to the water pot, to the hand pump. The headmaster muttered, "That one just wants attention. Send her off." Anjali watched Jaya's eyes flick to the gate whenever a motorbike passed; her father had gone to work in the city in June. So Anjali gave her a job, ringing the bell for recess, and a promise: "After you ring it, come and tell me." Each week she asked Jaya to carry the register a little farther, first to the next classroom, then alone to the office.

qa.q: What job did Anjali give Jaya?
qa.a: Ringing the bell for recess.

qa.q: What does Anjali seem to think about Jaya's clinginess?
qa.a: She is concerned rather than irritated, seeing Jaya's worry about the gate and her absent father instead of attention-seeking.

qa.q: How could Anjali keep helping Jaya grow more independent?
qa.a: Keep giving small tasks that take her a little farther away, with a steady promise to check back in.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya when the headmaster wants her sent off?
qa.a: Jaya might feel unwanted and more anxious, since what she needs is steady warmth while her father is away.

grounding: Shows a teacher who sees a clinging child's worry and responds with warmth and small steps towards independence.

passage: Since her grandmother moved back to Porto, Mina had started following Paulo from room to room in their Lisbon flat. She waited outside the bathroom. She asked at every meal, "You're picking me up today, right?" Paulo's brother laughed: "She's playing you. She wants attention." Paulo wasn't so sure. He noticed Mina asked most when her stomach hurt, or when he'd been on the phone a long time. So he started telling her the day's plan each morning, pickup time included, and gave her small missions: buy bread alone at the corner bakery while he waited outside. The first time she came out grinning, holding the loaf like a trophy.

qa.q: What did Mina ask at every meal?
qa.a: "You're picking me up today, right?"

qa.q: What was Paulo thinking when his brother called it attention-seeking?
qa.a: He was doubtful and concerned, noticing that Mina asked most when her stomach hurt, which suggested worry rather than a game.

qa.q: Which choice of Paulo's worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling her the plan each morning and giving small solo missions, because predictability and small wins build confidence.

qa.q: How might Mina feel coming out of the bakery with the loaf?
qa.a: She seems proud and delighted, having managed something alone while knowing Paulo was close.

grounding: Illustrates a parent reading clinginess as worry and answering with warmth and small independence steps.

passage: In the first week at the residential school, Santosh turned up at the warden's office door every evening at seven. "Ma'am, is the phone working? Can I call home?" Then: "Will you be here tomorrow?" Some seniors started calling him the warden's tail. Sharmila, the warden, had seen labels like that stick to kids before. She didn't send him off. Each night she said the same thing: "I'm here till ten, every day except Sunday." She set fixed calls home, Wednesdays and Saturdays. She asked him to help sort letters in the mailroom, beside her at first, then alone for ten minutes while she did rounds. By the third week he came by only on call nights.

qa.q: On which days could Santosh call home?
qa.a: Wednesdays and Saturdays.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when the seniors called Santosh the warden's tail?
qa.a: She was concerned, because she had seen such labels stick to kids, so she chose warmth instead of sending him away.

qa.q: What went right in Sharmila's plan?
qa.a: Same words each night, fixed call days and a small job done alone for longer stretches made the new place feel predictable.

qa.q: What is it like for Santosh in the first week?
qa.a: Santosh seems homesick and unsure, needing to check the phone and whether the warden will still be there.

grounding: Shows a warden who reads a new boarder's clinging as worry and offers steady warmth and small independence steps.

passage:
I'm Parveen, and I teach Class 4. This term I've been watching Farhan.
He follows me from the classroom to the staff room door. At recess he stands near the duty teacher instead of playing. He asks, "Ma'am, is my work okay?" four or five times a lesson, even when it's neat.
A colleague said, "He just wants attention." Maybe. But his hands twist his shirt while he waits for my answer, and he looks relieved each time I nod. I can't know what is going on inside him, but it doesn't look like a game.
So I've started saying, "Good morning, Farhan," warmly every day, and giving him small jobs he does alone: taking the register to the office, then watering the plants. Yesterday he did the plants and came back smiling, without asking once if it was okay.

qa.q: What small jobs does Parveen give Farhan?
qa.a: Taking the register to the office and watering the plants.

qa.q: What does Parveen feel about the colleague's "attention" comment?
qa.a: Parveen feels unsure and concerned rather than convinced, seeing Farhan's twisting hands and relief and thinking it doesn't look like a game.

qa.q: Why might the warm greeting and solo jobs help more than ignoring Farhan?
qa.a: They give him steady warmth he can count on while letting him practise small bits of independence, so he needs fewer reassurances.

qa.q: What might watering the plants alone be like for Farhan?
qa.a: He may feel proud and a little braver doing it by himself, which fits him coming back smiling without asking if it was okay.

grounding: Shows a teacher observing a child who shadows adults and seeks reassurance, choosing steady warmth and small independence steps over calling it attention-seeking.
